question.text: In the arrangement shown, block A has mass 4 kg and block B has mass 5 kg. Find the acceleration of each block.
conditions: upper pulley fixed to the ceiling
block A (4 kg) hangs from the right side of the string over the fixed pulley
block B (5 kg) hangs from the string over the movable pulley
one end of the movable-pulley's string is anchored near the fixed pulley's support

figure.description: A pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. A single light string passes over P₁: its right end hangs straight down to block A (4 kg). Its left end goes down, passes UNDER a small movable pulley P₂ (wrapping round its lower half) and comes back up to be tied to the fixed support of P₁, so P₂ hangs in a loop of that string with two vertical strands above it. Block B (5 kg) hangs directly from the axle of P₂ by a short string. Pulleys and strings are light and frictionless. When B moves down by x, A moves up by 2x.

solution.approach: A hangs from one strand; the movable pulley (holding B) has two strands, so aA = 2aB, opposite in direction; apply Newton's second law to each block.

steps.text: Take downward as positive for each block separately. The movable-pulley string constraint gives aA = −2aB.
Write Newton's second law for A (4 kg), held by a single strand of tension T.
Write Newton's second law for B (5 kg), held by two strands of tension T at the movable pulley.
aA is positive, so A accelerates downward at 20/7 m/s²; aB is negative, so B accelerates upward at 10/7 m/s², half the magnitude of aA, as the constraint requires.
steps.equation: A: 20/7 m/s² ≈ 2.9 m/s² down, B: 10/7 m/s² ≈ 1.4 m/s² up

final_answer.value: A (4 kg) accelerates at 20/7 m/s² ≈ 2.9 m/s² downward, and B (5 kg) accelerates at 10/7 m/s² ≈ 1.4 m/s² upward.

common_mistakes.text: Treating both blocks as hanging from a single strand of the same tension and using the plain Atwood formula (g(mA−mB)/(mA+mB)), which ignores the movable pulley.
Using only one strand of tension in the 5 kg block's equation instead of two, giving the wrong magnitude for both accelerations.
